title: Week 4 quiz: GPT and the tokenizer

questions.prompt: A training chunk is split into inputs and shifted targets. What does this print?
questions.code:
data = [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
block_size = 4
x = data[:block_size]
y = data[1:block_size + 1]
t = 2
print(x[:t + 1], "->", y[t])

options.rationale: The target is shifted by one; y[2] is data[3].
The model sees the whole prefix, not just the current token.
Position t = 2 sees x[0..2] and predicts y[2], the next token.
That's position t = 3.

questions.explanation: A chunk of block_size + 1 tokens gives block_size training examples, one per prefix length. The causal mask guarantees each position only uses its own prefix.

questions.prompt: This mask is meant to make attention causal. What does it actually do?
questions.code:
masked = [[scores[t][s] if s >= t else float("-inf") for s in range(T)]
          for t in range(T)]
weights = [softmax(row) for row in masked]

options.text: Each position attends to itself and *later* positions, so the model can read the token it is supposed to predict.
options.rationale: Keeping s >= t lets position t see the future. Training loss collapses, and generation fails because the future isn't there at sampling time.

options.text: It's correct: each position attends to itself and earlier positions.
options.rationale: The comparison is reversed.

options.text: Each position attends only to itself.
options.rationale: s >= t keeps every later position too.

options.text: It raises an error because -inf can't be passed to softmax.
options.rationale: exp(-inf) is 0, which is the point of using -inf.

questions.explanation: A reversed mask is a classic transformer bug because training looks great. The test from the lesson catches it: change tokens after position t and check that output t doesn't change.

options.rationale: Only ASCII characters are one byte in UTF-8.
Python's len on a str counts code points, not bytes.
Code points from U+0800 to U+FFFF, which include the euro sign (U+20AC), take three bytes.
The euro sign is one code point and three UTF-8 bytes; ASCII 'e' is one of each.

questions.explanation: A byte-level tokenizer starts from the bytes, so the euro sign begins as three base tokens until a merge combines them. This is part of why text outside a tokenizer's well-covered scripts costs more tokens.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of the residual connections (x + f(x)) in a transformer block?

options.text: They let tokens attend to future positions.
options.rationale: Masking controls that; residuals are per position.

options.text: They give gradients an identity path from the loss to early layers, so deep stacks stay trainable.
options.rationale: The derivative of x + f(x) with respect to x includes the identity, so gradient flows even if f's path is weak.

options.text: They normalize activations to unit variance.
options.rationale: That's LayerNorm's role.

options.text: They reduce the parameter count.
options.rationale: They add no parameters at all.

questions.explanation: Residual connections came from ResNets (He et al., 2015). In the lecture, adding them is what lets the model scale to more layers without training stalling.

questions.prompt: Which statements about LayerNorm, as used in the lecture's GPT, are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It behaves the same in training and inference.
options.rationale: There are no batch statistics, so there are no running estimates and no mode switch.

options.text: In the lecture's pre-norm arrangement it is applied before attention and before the feed-forward layer in each block.
options.rationale: That follows GPT-2, whose paper moved layer norm to the input of each sub-block.

options.text: It requires a batch size larger than 1.
options.rationale: It works on a single token vector.

options.text: It normalizes each token's vector across its features, independently of other examples in the batch.
options.rationale: That's the difference from BatchNorm, which normalizes each feature across the batch.

questions.explanation: Removing batch dependence is one reason transformers use LayerNorm: generation often runs one sequence at a time, and examples shouldn't influence each other.

questions.prompt: You train a character-level GPT on CPU with nanoGPT-like small settings (4 layers, 4 heads, 128-dim embeddings, context 64). After a few minutes your validation loss is 0.9, far better than the roughly 1.88 nanoGPT's README reports for a similar CPU config on Shakespeare. Samples look poor. What do you suspect first?

options.text: Your implementation is simply better; write it up.
options.rationale: A result this far from a published baseline on similar settings is more likely a bug than a breakthrough.

options.text: The learning rate is too low.
options.rationale: A low learning rate would make the loss worse, not better.

options.text: Leakage: a broken causal mask letting positions see their targets, or validation text overlapping the training text.
options.rationale: Both make validation loss look excellent while generation, which has no future tokens to peek at, stays poor.

options.text: The tokenizer is too small.
options.rationale: A character vocabulary is standard for this setup.

questions.explanation: Calibrate against a known baseline before trusting a surprising number. Check the mask with a test (changing future tokens must not change earlier outputs) and check that the validation split is a separate, contiguous region of text. Different corpora also have different achievable losses, so compare like with like.

questions.prompt: This BPE `encode` sometimes produces token sequences that the trained model has never seen, even for text from the training corpus. Why?

options.text: It should start from code points, not bytes.
options.rationale: Byte-level BPE correctly starts from UTF-8 bytes.

options.text: `merge` should be applied right to left.
options.rationale: Direction isn't the issue; the choice of which pair to merge is.

options.text: It never terminates.
options.rationale: It stops when the most frequent pair isn't in merges, or when one token is left.

options.text: It merges the most frequent pair in the *input*, instead of the pair with the lowest merge rank, so merges can be applied in a different order than training learned them.
options.rationale: Later merges are built from earlier ones; applying them out of order can produce different (still decodable) tokenizations.

questions.explanation: Encoding must replay training: repeatedly apply the learned merge with the lowest id that appears in the sequence. Out-of-order encoding still round-trips through decode, which is why a round-trip test alone doesn't catch it; also test that encoding matches a reference implementation.

options.rationale: The 1 at index 4 is followed by another 1, not a 2.
Scanning left to right: (1,2) merges, (1,2) merges, the lone 1 stays, then (1,2) merges.
The final 1, 2 pair is merged too.
The sequence starts with the pair 1, 2.

questions.explanation: Merging scans once, left to right, without overlaps. Getting this function exactly right matters because training, encoding, and every round-trip test depend on it.
